elude|hedge.distinction: To elude a question is to slip away from it entirely, while to hedge is to answer in terms that commit to nothing.

elusive|evasive.distinction: An elusive idea is hard to pin down by its nature, while an evasive witness is dodging on purpose.

eminent|lofty.distinction: An eminent scholar is distinguished by achievement, while a lofty manner looks down on everyone from a height.

enchant|enrapture.distinction: To enchant is to charm as if by a spell, while to enrapture is to carry someone away in delight.

enchant|enthrall.distinction: To enchant someone is to charm them, while to enthrall them is to hold their attention so completely nothing else registers.

encomium|eulogy.distinction: An encomium praises anyone worth honouring, while a eulogy is usually delivered over someone who has died.

encomium|paean.distinction: An encomium is formal praise in prose, while a paean is a song of praise and triumph.

encomium|panegyric.distinction: An encomium and a panegyric are both formal praise; panegyric suggests the more elaborate and public of the two.

endemic|indigenous.distinction: A disease is endemic where it is always present, while a plant is indigenous where it originated; presence against origin.

enervate|unnerve.distinction: To enervate someone is to drain their physical energy, while to unnerve them is to drain their confidence.

engender|generate.distinction: To engender resentment is to bring it into being over time, while to generate power is to produce it directly.

enrapture|enthrall.distinction: To enrapture is to fill someone with delight, while to enthrall is to hold their attention captive.

enthrall|mesmerize.distinction: To enthrall is to hold attention completely, while to mesmerize suggests the fixed stare of someone under hypnosis.

ephemeral|evanescent.distinction: Ephemeral things live briefly by their nature, while evanescent things fade away as you watch them.

ephemeral|transient.distinction: Ephemeral suggests a lifespan measured in a day, while transient simply means passing through and not staying.

ephemeral|transitory.distinction: Ephemeral stresses how briefly a thing lives, while transitory stresses that it is a stage on the way to something else.

epitome|paradigm.distinction: An epitome is the purest single example of a type, while a paradigm is the framework that type is understood through.

equable|placid.distinction: An equable temper stays level whatever happens, while a placid one is calm because nothing disturbs it in the first place.

equivocate|prevaricate.distinction: To equivocate is to use words that could mean either thing, while to prevaricate is to dodge the truth by any means.

erratic|fickle.distinction: Erratic behaviour is unpredictable in any direction, while fickle affection is unpredictable specifically in loyalty.

erratic|mercurial.distinction: Erratic describes behaviour that follows no pattern, while mercurial describes a mood that swings fast and far.

esoteric|recondite.distinction: Esoteric knowledge is confined to a small circle, while recondite knowledge is simply too deep for most readers to follow.

establish|institute.distinction: To establish a practice is to set it up so it lasts, while to institute one is to start it off by formal act.

eulogy|paean.distinction: A eulogy honours someone, usually at a funeral, while a paean celebrates a triumph in song.

eulogy|panegyric.distinction: A eulogy is praise spoken for a person, often the dead, while a panegyric is elaborate formal praise for anything.

evade|hedge.distinction: To evade a question is to get around answering it, while to hedge is to answer in a way that commits to nothing.

evident|manifest.distinction: Evident means the fact can be seen once you look, while manifest means it is showing itself plainly without looking.

evident|palpable.distinction: Evident describes what is plain to see, while palpable describes a tension so thick you could almost touch it.

evident|patent.distinction: Evident and patent both mean obvious; patent carries the stronger note of something nobody could possibly dispute.

evoke|invoke.distinction: To evoke a memory is to call it up in someone, while to invoke a rule is to call on it for authority.

evoke|kindle.distinction: To evoke a feeling is to summon one that already existed, while to kindle one is to start it from nothing.

evoke|provoke.distinction: To evoke sympathy is to draw it out gently, while to provoke anger is to stir it up deliberately.

exacerbate|exasperate.distinction: You exacerbate a problem by making it worse, and exasperate a person by wearing their patience through.

exacting|stringent.distinction: An exacting supervisor demands great care from people, while stringent rules demand strict compliance from everyone.

exalt|extol.distinction: To exalt someone is to raise them in rank or honour, while to extol them is to praise them in words.

exalt|inspire.distinction: To exalt is to lift someone in standing or spirit, while to inspire is to fill them with the urge to act.

exalt|invigorate.distinction: To exalt is to raise up in honour, while to invigorate is to put fresh physical energy into someone.

exalt|laud.distinction: To exalt is to raise someone high in rank or esteem, while to laud is simply to praise them warmly.

excise|expunge.distinction: To excise a passage is to cut it out of the text, while to expunge it is to erase it so no trace remains.

excoriate|objurgate.distinction: To excoriate is to flay someone publicly with criticism, while to objurgate is to deliver a severe scolding.

excruciating|harrowing.distinction: Excruciating pain is felt in the body, while a harrowing experience tears at the mind.

exculpate|exonerate.distinction: To exculpate is to clear someone of blame by argument, while to exonerate is the formal clearing of a charge.

execrable|odious.distinction: Execrable describes something so bad it deserves cursing, while odious describes something that provokes disgust.

execrable|woeful.distinction: Execrable quality invites curses, while woeful quality invites lament; both are bad, one enrages and one saddens.

execrate|loathe.distinction: To execrate is to curse something aloud, while to loathe is to hate it deeply without saying a word.

exertion|travail.distinction: Exertion is effort that costs energy, while travail is effort that costs pain and hardship.

exhaustive|thorough.distinction: An exhaustive search covers every possible case, while a thorough one is careful about each case it does cover.

exorbitant|unconscionable.distinction: An exorbitant price is far higher than the thing is worth, while an unconscionable one offends against decency itself.

expatiate|expound.distinction: To expatiate is to go on at length, while to expound is to explain systematically; length against exposition.

expel|oust.distinction: To expel someone is to drive them out of a place, while to oust them is to remove them from a position they held.

exponent|proponent.distinction: An exponent represents a style by practising it, while a proponent argues for a cause without necessarily doing it.

extemporaneous|offhand.distinction: Extemporaneous remarks are unrehearsed but still serious, while offhand ones are unrehearsed and casually dismissive.

extemporize|improvise.distinction: To extemporize is to speak without preparation, while to improvise is to make anything from whatever is at hand.

extol|laud.distinction: To extol and to laud are both to praise; extol carries more enthusiasm, laud more formality.

extort|gouge.distinction: To extort money is to take it by threat, while to gouge a customer is to take it by an outrageous price.

extraneous|impertinent.distinction: Extraneous material simply does not belong, while impertinent behaviour is rude as well as beside the point.

extrapolate|infer.distinction: To extrapolate is to carry a trend beyond the data, while to infer is to draw a conclusion from the data you have.

extravagant|exuberant.distinction: Extravagant spending goes beyond what is reasonable, while exuberant energy simply overflows.

extravagant|overweening.distinction: Extravagant describes excess in spending or display, while overweening describes excess in pride and self-regard.

extravagant|prodigal.distinction: Extravagant spending is showy, while prodigal spending squanders a fortune until nothing is left.

extravagant|profligate.distinction: Extravagant means spending far too much, while profligate adds recklessness and a loss of all restraint.

extravagant|spendthrift.distinction: Extravagant describes the spending, while a spendthrift is the person doing it; adjective against noun.

exuberant|luxuriant.distinction: Exuberant describes people full of energy, while luxuriant describes vegetation growing thickly.

exuberant|overweening.distinction: Exuberant energy is high spirits overflowing, while overweening pride is self-regard overreaching.

exuberant|profuse.distinction: Exuberant describes lively energy, while profuse describes sheer quantity poured out.

fawning|obsequious.distinction: Fawning attention flatters to win favour, while obsequious service is servile in every gesture.

fawn|grovel.distinction: To fawn is to flatter with an eye on advantage, while to grovel is to abase oneself outright.

fawn|kowtow.distinction: To fawn is to flatter a superior, while to kowtow is to defer so completely that no disagreement is possible.

fawn|toady.distinction: To fawn is what the flattering is called, while a toady is the person who makes a habit of it.

feasible|viable.distinction: A feasible plan can be carried out, while a viable one can survive on its own once it has been.

fervent|fervid.distinction: Fervent feeling is admired for its warmth, while fervid feeling runs so hot it becomes uncomfortable.

fervent|torrid.distinction: Fervent describes passionate conviction, while torrid describes heat, whether of climate or of an affair.

fervent|zealous.distinction: Fervent describes the warmth of the feeling, while zealous describes the energy poured into acting on it.

fervid|torrid.distinction: Fervid heat is emotional and often excessive, while torrid heat is literal or sexual.

fervor|zeal.distinction: Fervor is the heat of the feeling itself, while zeal is that heat turned into tireless action for a cause.

fetid|malodorous.distinction: Fetid suggests the rotting smell of stagnant matter, while malodorous is the neutral formal word for any bad smell.

fetid|noisome.distinction: Fetid points squarely at a rotting stench, while noisome covers anything offensive, smell included.

filch|pilfer.distinction: To filch is to take one small thing on impulse, while to pilfer is to take small things repeatedly.

financial|monetary.distinction: Financial matters concern money and its management, while monetary policy concerns the currency and its supply.

financial|pecuniary.distinction: Financial is the everyday word for money matters, while pecuniary is the formal one, common in law.

flair|panache.distinction: Flair is a natural talent for something, while panache is the flamboyant confidence with which it is displayed.

fledgling|neophyte.distinction: A fledgling enterprise is new and untested, while a neophyte is a person newly come to a practice.

fleece|swindle.distinction: To fleece someone is to overcharge them steadily, while to swindle them is to cheat them by outright deception.

fleeting|momentary.distinction: A fleeting glimpse passes before you can hold it, while a momentary pause lasts a moment and then ends.

flip|impudent.distinction: A flip answer treats a serious question lightly, while an impudent one is boldly disrespectful to the asker.

flip|insolent.distinction: Flip remarks are casually disrespectful, while insolent ones carry open contempt for the person addressed.

florid|sanguine.distinction: Florid describes a red complexion or overwrought prose, while sanguine describes a cheerfully optimistic outlook.

flout|gibe.distinction: To flout a rule is to break it openly, while a gibe is a mocking remark aimed at a person.

flout|scoff.distinction: To flout a rule is to disobey it in plain view, while to scoff is to speak of it with derision.

fluctuate|vacillate.distinction: Prices fluctuate by rising and falling, while a person vacillates by wavering between two decisions.

flush|heyday.distinction: Flush describes being well supplied with money right now, while a heyday is the whole period when things went best.

foible|idiosyncrasy.distinction: A foible is a small weakness of character, while an idiosyncrasy is simply a habit peculiar to one person.

foil|frustrate.distinction: To foil a plot is to block it at the moment of execution, while to frustrate a plan is to wear it down until it fails.

foil|thwart.distinction: To foil and to thwart both mean to stop a plan; foil suggests a single decisive block, thwart a sustained obstruction.

foolhardy|heady.distinction: Foolhardy describes recklessness that courts disaster, while heady describes excitement that goes to the head.

foolhardy|rash.distinction: A rash act is done without thinking, while a foolhardy one is done knowing the danger and going ahead anyway.

forbear|forebear.distinction: To forbear is to hold back from doing something, while a forebear is an ancestor; one is a verb, the other a person.

foreboding|presentiment.distinction: Foreboding is the sense that something bad is coming, while a presentiment is a feeling about what is coming, good or ill.

foreshadow|portend.distinction: A detail foreshadows an event by hinting at it early, while a sign portends one by warning that it is on the way.

forestall|preclude.distinction: To forestall something is to act first so it never happens, while to preclude it is to rule it out in advance.
